hero.title: Valve Decoder
hero.subtitle: A Python application that turns FlowSafe's historical PDF pick-sheets into a structured, searchable engineering database.
hero.factline: Role: Industrial Engineering Intern · FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions · Continuing during the academic semester

blocks.heading: Problem
blocks.body: FlowSafe's historical shipped-valve records existed only as PDF pick-sheets: a format that's fine for a single job, but effectively unusable as a data source once you need to search, aggregate, or analyze across thousands of them.

blocks.heading: Why it mattered
blocks.body: The facility material-flow analysis needed reliable historical valve-shipment data to calculate accurate travel-path frequencies between facility locations. That data existed, but it was locked inside thousands of individual PDF documents with no structured or searchable form. The facility study could not move forward until a real dataset existed.

blocks.heading: Constraints
items: No clean structured export of the historical pick-sheet data existed: only the original PDFs.
The extracted data needed to be accurate enough to support a real quantitative analysis, not just a rough approximation.
Needed to be general enough to stay useful as a reference tool after the immediate need (the facility study) was done.

blocks.heading: My role
blocks.body: I built the Valve Decoder independently as my project during my Industrial Engineering internship at FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions.

blocks.heading: Data & engineering approach
items: Built a Python application to parse historical PDF pick-sheets and extract structured records.
Processed 19,567 shipped-valve records covering 1,951 unique valve models.
Structured the extracted data into a searchable database, rather than a one-off export.

blocks.heading: Development process
blocks.body: I built the PDF-parsing and data-extraction pipeline first, validated the extracted records for accuracy against the source documents, then structured the output into a searchable database: usable both for the immediate facility material-flow analysis and as a standalone engineering reference tool afterward.

blocks.heading: Solution
blocks.body: A Python application that converts FlowSafe's historical PDF pick-sheets into a structured, searchable database of shipped-valve records: closing the data gap that was blocking the facility material-flow study, and outliving that original purpose as a reusable production/engineering reference tool.

blocks.heading: What I learned
blocks.body: I learned that a lot of useful data is not actually missing, it is just trapped in a format that makes it hard to use. The important part was not only extracting the records, but validating and structuring them well enough that other engineering work could depend on them. Building the Valve Decoder also showed me the value of designing past the immediate assignment, what started as a way to unblock the facility study became a tool people could continue using as an engineering reference.

hero.title: Facility Material Flow & Layout Analysis
hero.subtitle: Two years of operational data and a scaled AutoCAD facility model, turned into a quantified case for how FlowSafe's production, cleaning, testing, and storage areas should be arranged.
hero.factline: Role: Industrial Engineering Intern · FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions · Continuing during the academic semester

blocks.heading: Problem
blocks.body: FlowSafe's facility layout had developed over time without a data-driven relayout. That included the placement of production, cleaning, testing, and point-of-use storage areas. No one had a quantified picture of how much material and people movement the existing layout actually required, so there was no basis for saying which layout changes would meaningfully help versus which would just move the problem around.

blocks.heading: Why it mattered
blocks.body: Every job that moves through the facility pays a travel cost between areas, from production to cleaning, testing, storage, and back. That cost repeats on every job, every day. Without a quantified baseline, layout decisions were effectively guesses. Establishing a real, data-backed measure of transportation effort was the precondition for making a defensible case for any layout change at all.

blocks.heading: Constraints
items: Had to work within FlowSafe's existing building footprint: this is a relayout study, not new construction.
Had to preserve required adjacencies between production, cleaning, and testing rather than optimize travel distance in isolation.
Recommendations needed to be justified by a quantified model, not intuition, to be actionable for management.
Needed to hold up against two years of real operational variation, not a single snapshot in time.

blocks.heading: My role
blocks.body: I analyzed the operational data, built the scaled AutoCAD facility model, and developed the transportation-effort analysis independently as my project during my Industrial Engineering internship at FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions.

blocks.heading: Data & engineering approach
items: Built a scaled AutoCAD model of the facility covering 104 distinct activity locations.
Constructed the full set of origin-destination travel paths between those locations from two years of production/operational data: 10,816 paths in total.
Applied a distance × movement-frequency transportation-effort model to quantify how much effort the current layout requires, giving a current-state baseline to test future layouts against.
Used the Valve Decoder database to close data gaps in the historical valve-shipment records feeding this analysis.

blocks.heading: Development process
blocks.body: I built the current-state model first by mapping all 104 activity locations and calculating baseline transportation effort from the historical travel-path data. I then tested changes to production-area placement, cleaning-area placement, testing-capacity allocation, and point-of-use storage. I recalculated modeled transportation effort for each scenario until arriving at a recommended future-state layout.

blocks.heading: Solution
blocks.body: A recommended future-state facility layout with specific changes to production-area organization, cleaning-area placement, testing-capacity allocation, and point-of-use storage locations: every recommendation justified by the same distance × frequency effort model used to establish the current-state baseline, so the comparison between current and future state is apples-to-apples.

blocks.heading: What I learned
blocks.body: I learned how much stronger a layout recommendation becomes when the current problem is measured before anything is moved. Using the same transportation-effort model for every option made the comparison clear, but the lowest number was not automatically the best real-world layout. I still had to account for how production, cleaning, testing, storage, and the people working in those areas actually interact.

hero.title: Digital Pressure-Testing System
hero.subtitle: A connected digital pressure-testing and reporting ecosystem that runs from the operator station to the manager dashboard. It replaces paper-based valve testing with a guided, centrally recorded digital workflow.
hero.factline: Role: Industrial Engineering Intern · FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions · Continuing during the academic semester

blocks.heading: Problem
blocks.body: Valve pressure testing at FlowSafe relied on physical dial gauges and manual, paper-based recordkeeping. Results from procedures such as the three-pop and bubble tests existed only as handwritten records tied to a single physical location. There was no centralized digital record, stored pressure trace, or live visibility into test-stand activity from outside the test area.

blocks.heading: Why it mattered
blocks.body: Every test still required a technician to run the procedure, then separately transcribe results into paperwork for the Functional Test Report (FTR) and other downstream documentation. Testing and documenting the same test as separate tasks consumed technician and administrative time on every valve that shipped. Managers also had no way to see test-stand status without physically walking the floor.

blocks.heading: Constraints
items: Had to work on the shop floor, integrated with existing physical digital pressure gauges rather than replacing them.
Had to preserve FlowSafe's existing test procedures (three-pop testing, bubble-test workflows) rather than change the underlying engineering process.
Had to support the existing Functional Test Report (FTR) output that downstream documentation depends on.
Full ERP integration was out of scope: the system needed to lay a read-only foundation for a future Epicor integration, not replace or write into Epicor.

blocks.heading: My role
blocks.body: I developed the system as my project during my Industrial Engineering internship at FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions: from the operator-station hardware and guided testing workflow through the centralized data model and the manager-facing dashboard.

blocks.heading: Data & engineering approach
items: Raspberry Pi operator stations at the test stands, connected to the physical digital pressure gauges for live pressure capture during a test.

Guided, on-screen operator workflows that walk a technician through the correct testing sequence, including the three-pop and bubble-test procedures, instead of relying on memory or a paper checklist.
Every test tagged with operator, job, and valve identification, and its full pressure trace stored against a centralized test record rather than a handwritten sheet.
A manager-facing dashboard giving live visibility into test-stand status, independent of walking the floor.

blocks.heading: Development process
blocks.body: I built the system incrementally on the shop floor: standing up an operator station and gauge integration first, then layering in the guided workflow, the centralized test-record database and pressure-trace storage, and the manager dashboard on top of that same data. Functional Test Report support and the read-only Epicor integration foundation were built to sit on the same central record, so the live test data, the FTR, and the future ERP link all trace back to one source instead of three separate, disconnected records.

blocks.heading: Solution
blocks.body: The result is a connected pressure-testing ecosystem: operators run guided tests at Raspberry Pi stations wired to the physical digital gauges, every test is captured with its full pressure trace and operator/job/valve identification, and that record is centralized rather than sitting on paper. Managers get live visibility into test-stand activity, the Functional Test Report draws from the same recorded data, and the system has a read-only foundation in place for a future Epicor connection.

blocks.body: I learned that a shop-floor system only works if it fits the way operators already do the job. Starting with the physical gauge and the testing sequence helped me build the digital workflow around the process instead of forcing the process around the software. I also learned to treat the hardware, operator experience, stored test data, reporting, and management visibility as one connected system rather than separate features.

hero.title: Sales Workflow & Epicor Integration Platform
hero.subtitle: A centralized, auditable sales workflow connecting pre-Epicor work, historical records, and live read-only Epicor data.
hero.factline: Role: Designer & developer · Business systems integration · 2026

blocks.heading: The workflow gap
blocks.body: A small inside-sales team needed to track work received before it was formally entered in Epicor. Spreadsheet and email tracking fragmented status, ownership, and history, while the production system required strict controls. The goal was a useful operational layer that connected to Epicor without writing to or weakening the production system.

blocks.heading: A controlled integration boundary
blocks.body: The platform uses read-only access for Epicor customer, quote, sales-order, and quote-workflow information. Provisional customer identities support early work, then link conservatively to Epicor identities when validated. Immutable FlowSafe reference numbers keep the internal record stable through those linkage changes.

blocks.heading: Implemented workflow
items: Centralized tracking for requests received before formal Epicor entry.
Global duplicate-PO prevention across provisional and Epicor-linked records.
Automatic PO-to-sales-order matching using conservative validation rules.
Quote-conversion detection and at-risk alerts when expected sales orders are missing.
A reconciliation worker that checks linkage state every 15 minutes.
History and audit records for important identity and transaction-linkage changes.

blocks.heading: Historical reconciliation
blocks.note: Counts are approximate. No customer data, credentials, internal URLs, employee data, or proprietary records are shown here.

blocks.heading: Safe staged implementation
blocks.body: Production implementation was staged deliberately: historical data was reconciled first, matches were accepted only when validation rules were satisfied, and ambiguous records remained visible for review rather than being forced into a link. The platform centralizes workflow without treating automation as permission to guess.

blocks.heading: Outcome
items: One auditable place to track pre-Epicor sales work.
Clear continuity between provisional records and live Epicor customers, quotes, and sales orders.
Earlier visibility into missing sales orders and quote-conversion risk.
A controlled integration pattern that preserves production-system boundaries.

blocks.heading: What I learned
blocks.body: I learned that connecting systems is as much about deciding what should not happen automatically as it is about moving data between them. Keeping Epicor access read-only, making uncertain matches visible for review, and preserving an audit trail made the workflow safer and more useful. The project reinforced that good automation should remove repetitive work without hiding uncertainty or taking control away from the people responsible for the process.

hero.title: V.A.L.V.E.-E. Interactive Tutorial & Internal Assistant
hero.subtitle: A consistent tutorial character across the FlowSafe application, with a broader controlled internal assistant still in development.
hero.factline: Role: Interaction design & development · Manufacturing UX · 2026

blocks.heading: Why a tutorial character
blocks.body: The FlowSafe application spans tools for operators, engineers, and managers. V.A.L.V.E.-E. gives that system a consistent, approachable guide so users do not have to discover every page, control, and workflow unaided.

blocks.heading: Current Role
items: Appears throughout the application as a consistent tutorial character.
Introduces individual pages and explains their purpose.
Guides users toward important controls, workflows, and available actions.
Uses page-specific tutorial content instead of one generic walkthrough.
Supports onboarding while providing a consistent personality and visual identity.

blocks.heading: Current tutorial identity
blocks.caption: The character artwork is used across page-specific tutorials; sensitive application screens are not shown.

blocks.heading: In Development
items: The capabilities below are developed or partially integrated, not represented as fully production-ready.
FTR and job lookup capabilities.
Test-stand availability and read-only pressure-test information lookup.
Valve Decoder access and Engineering Viewer navigation.
Controlled internal knowledge sources, role-aware behavior, allowlisted navigation, and audit logging.
Multiple audience and persona concepts for different internal users.

blocks.heading: Safe assistant direction
blocks.body: The longer-term direction is a unified internal assistant for locating information and navigating manufacturing tools safely. Continued work focuses on controlled documentation retrieval, contextual guidance based on page, role, and task, and careful integration with the pressure-testing and engineering ecosystem.

blocks.heading: Design principles
items: Guide rather than overwhelm.
Use controlled, role-appropriate sources.
Keep navigation allowlisted and actions auditable.
Clearly distinguish available behavior from work in progress.
Never expose credentials, proprietary records, or sensitive internal screens.

blocks.heading: Technologies & tools
items: Human–Computer Interaction
Page-specific tutorial design
Manufacturing UX
Role-aware behavior
Controlled knowledge sources
Allowlisted navigation
Audit logging

blocks.heading: What I learned
blocks.body: I learned that guidance works best when it appears in the context of the task instead of asking users to remember one large walkthrough. Giving V.A.L.V.E.-E. a consistent personality makes the system feel more approachable, but the assistant still needs clear boundaries around its sources, navigation, and role-specific behavior. That balance between personality and control is what makes an internal assistant helpful without making it distracting or unsafe.
